tip: With a negative verb, ‘pek’ means not really rather than very: ‘pek beğenmedi’, did not really like it.
‘ne’ with ‘ne de’ means neither nor: ‘ne çay ne de kahve’, neither tea nor coffee, and the verb itself stays positive.
Add ‘-ken’ for while at the same time: ‘yağ’ (fall or snow) plus ‘arken’ gives ‘yağarken’, while it was snowing.
‘bir yandan’ with ‘öte yandan’ sets up two sides: on one hand the pay, on the other hand the hours.
For a real, likely condition use aorist plus ‘-sa’: ‘kazan’ (win) plus ‘ır’ plus ‘sak’ gives ‘kazanırsak’, if we win.
‘keşke’ (if only) pairs with the ‘-saydı’ past to voice a regret: ‘keşke çalışsaydım’, I wish I had studied.
Verb plus ‘-madan önce’ means before doing: ‘yatmadan önce’, before going to bed, and the verb carries no tense.
Add ‘-dığında’ to a verb for when it happened: ‘yağdığında’, when it snowed.
The causative ‘-dır’ makes someone gain something: ‘kazan’ (gain) plus ‘dır’ gives ‘kazandırmak’, to make gain or instill.
The ‘-alım’ ending makes a let us suggestion, here negative: ‘unutmayalım’, let us not forget.
‘ait’ (belonging to) takes the dative on the word before it: ‘dönemine ait’, belonging to the period.
‘kaçırmamalıyız’ means must not miss. The ‘-malı’ is the must part, and the ‘-ma-’ right before it makes it negative.
‘koşabildiğin kadar’ means as fast as you can run. ‘-abil’ marks ability, and ‘kadar’ sets the as much as limit.
‘pişirdiğin yemek’ means the food you cooked. The ‘-diğin’ ending makes a verb describe the noun right after it.
‘yarına kadar’ means by tomorrow. ‘kadar’ needs the dative ‘-a’ on the time word, giving ‘yarına’ from ‘yarın’.
‘arabayla’ means by car. The ‘-yla’ ending marks the means you use; the ‘y’ is just a buffer after the vowel.
‘babaannemden’ means from my grandmother. The ‘-den’ ending marks the source that something comes from.
‘söyler misiniz’ is a polite request. The aorist ‘söyler’ plus the question ‘misiniz’ softens it to could you tell.
‘yerinde olsam’ sets an unreal if with ‘-sa’, and ‘ederdim’ answers it with the would ending ‘-erdi’.
‘geldiğinde’ means when he arrives. The ‘-diğinde’ ending on a verb builds a when clause.
‘akşamleyin’ means in the evening. The ‘-leyin’ ending turns a time word into an at that time adverb.
‘unutmasaydım’ means if I hadn't forgotten. The ‘-masaydı’ ending builds an unreal condition about the past.
‘önce’ meaning before takes the ablative ‘-ten’: ‘yemekten önce’ means before the meal.
‘çıkınca’ means when it broke out, or as soon as it did. The ‘-ınca’ ending links one action right before another.
‘açmış’ uses ‘-mış’ for something noticed after the fact: the flowers have bloomed, going by what you see now.
‘göre’ meaning according to takes the dative ‘-e’: ‘haberlere göre’ means according to the news.
‘beri’ meaning since takes the ablative ‘-tan’: ‘sabahtan beri’ means since the morning.
‘yardım etmek’ takes the dative for who gets helped: ‘yaşlılara’ means to the elderly, with the dative ‘-a’ on ‘yaşlılar’.
‘taşınmayı’ turns the verb move into an object: ‘-ma’ makes it a noun, ‘-yı’ marks it as what they plan.
‘tamir etmemiz gerekiyor’ means we need to fix it. ‘-memiz’ carries the we, and ‘gerekiyor’ adds the need.
